To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

exposure to elevated levels of particulate air pollution is associated, in a dose-dependent manner, with smaller brain volume and higher odds of covert infarcts in a large cohort of older persons free of dementia and prior stroke.

long-term exposure to elevated levels of air pollution was associated with smaller brain volume, a measure of age-associated brain volume loss, and with higher prevalence of brain infarcts in cognitively intact older adults.
Long-term exposure to air pollution was associated with smaller brain volumes and increased risk of small brain infarcts in cognitively normal persons.
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding the impact of air pollution exposure on brain health.
understanding the effects of long-term exposure to air pollution on brain aging in a population-based sample of elderly individuals free of dementia and clinical stroke.
the effects of air pollution on brain structure and function.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the study by Mortensen et al. (1) provides evidence of an association between air pollution and brain structure, but the study is not without limitations and does not provide conclusive evidence that air pollution causes changes in brain structure.
air pollution exposure is associated with brain atrophy and covert brain infarcst.
long term exposure to air pollution may be associated with smaller brain size, and with higher risk of brain infarcts, but not white matter hyperintensities.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

long-term exposure to fine particulate matter is associated with smaller total brain volume and higher odds of covert infarcts, while residential proximity to major roads is associated with greater white matter hyperintensities.
long-term exposure to elevated levels of fine particulate matter (PM2.5) and living close to major roads are associated with smaller total brain volume and higher odds of covert infarcts.
long-term exposure to air pollution is associated in an adverse manner with structural brain aging.
The main takeaway from our work is that
long-term exposure to fine particulate matter and proximity to major road traffic are both associated with smaller brain volume and higher risk of covert infarcts.
air pollution is a risk factor for structural brain changes in the aging population.
long-term exposure to air pollution may be related to structural changes to the brain.
